title: Mayrah, the Wind That Blows the Winter Away
title_raw: MAYRAH, THE WIND THAT BLOWS THE WINTER AWAY
culture_region: オーストラリア先住民
year_evidence: 扉に版年の刻みが無い。序文の署名が『K. LANGLOH PARKER, BANGATE, NARRAN RIVER, NEW SOUTH WALES, June 24th, 1895.』
book_title: Australian Legendary Tales: folk-lore of the Noongahburrahs as told to the Piccaninnies
source_title: Australian Legendary Tales: folk-lore of the Noongahburrahs as told to the Piccaninnies
text:
At the beginning of winter, the iguanas hide themselves in their homes
in the sand; the black eagle hawks go into their nests; the garbarlee
or shingle-backs hide themselves in little logs, just big enough to
hold them; the iguanas dig a long way into the sand and cover up the
passage behind them, as they go along. They all stay in their winter
homes until Mayrah blows the winter away. Mayrah first blows up a
thunderstorm. When the iguanas hear the thunder, they know the spring
is not far off, so they begin making a passage to go out again, but
they do not leave their winter home until the Curreequinquin, or
butcher birds sing all day almost without ceasing "Goore, goore, goore,
goore." Then they know that Mayrah has really blown the winter away,
for the birds are beginning to pair and build their nests. So they open
their eyes and come out on the green earth again. And when the black
fellows hear the curreequinquins singing "Goore, goore," they know that
they can go out and find iguanas again, and find them fatter than when
they went away with the coming of winter. Then, too, will they find
piggiebillahs hurrying along to get away from their young ones, which
they have buried in the sand and left to shift for themselves, for no
longer can they carry them, as the spines of the young ones begin to
prick them in their pouch. So they leave them and hurry away, that they
may not hear their cry. They know they shall meet them again later on,
when they are grown big. Then as Mayrah softly blows, the flowers one
by one open, and the bees come out again to gather honey. Every bird
wears his gayest plumage and sings his sweetest song to attract a mate,
and in pairs they go to build their nests. And still Mayrah softly
blows until the land is one of plenty; then Yhi the sun chases her back
whence she came, and the flowers droop and the birds sing only in the
early morning. For Yhi rules in the land until the storms are over and
have cooled him, and winter takes his place to be blown away again by
Mayrah the loved of all, and the bringer of plenty.

They all stay in their winter homes until Mayrah blows the winter away. Mayrah first blows up a thunderstorm. When the iguanas hear the thunder, they know the spring is not far off, so they begin making a passage to go out again, but they do not leave their winter home until the Curreequinquin, or butcher birds sing all day almost without ceasing "Goore, goore, goore, goore." Then they know that Mayrah has really blown the winter away, for the birds are beginning to pair and build their nests. So they open their eyes and come out on the green earth again. And when the black fellows hear the curreequinquins singing "Goore, goore," they know that they can go out and find iguanas again, and find them fatter than when they went away with the coming of winter. Then, too, will they find piggiebillahs hurrying along to get away from their young ones, which they have buried in the sand and left to shift for themselves, for no longer can they carry them, as the spines of the young ones begin to prick them in their pouch. So they leave them and hurry away, that they may not hear their cry. They know they shall meet them again later on, when they are grown big. Then as Mayrah softly blows, the flowers one by one open, and the bees come out again to gather honey. Every bird wears his gayest plumage and sings his sweetest song to attract a mate, and in pairs they go to build their nests. And still Mayrah softly blows until the land is one of plenty; then Yhi the sun chases her back whence she came, and the flowers droop and the birds sing only in the early morning. For Yhi rules in the land until the storms are over and have cooled him, and winter takes his place to be blown away again by Mayrah the loved of all, and the bringer of plenty.

冬の初めになると、イグアナは砂の中の住み処に身を隠し、黒いオナガイヌワシは巣にこもり、ガーバーリー、すなわちマツカサトカゲは、ちょうど身の入るほどの小さな丸太に隠れる。イグアナは砂の奥深くまで掘り進み、進みながら後ろの通り道を覆ってふさぐ。みな、メイラーが冬を吹き払うまで冬の住み処にとどまる。メイラーはまず雷雨を吹き起こす。雷を聞くとイグアナたちは、春が遠くないと知って、また出るための通り道を作り始める。けれどもクリークインクイン、すなわちモズガラスが一日じゅうほとんど休みなく「グーレ、グーレ、グーレ、グーレ」と歌うまでは、冬の住み処を離れない。そのとき初めて、メイラーが本当に冬を吹き払ったと知る。鳥たちが番いになり巣を作り始めるからである。そこで目を開けて、ふたたび緑の大地へ出て来る。そして人々はクリークインクインが「グーレ、グーレ」と歌うのを聞くと、また出かけてイグアナを見つけられると知る。しかも冬の訪れとともに姿を消したときより太っているのである。そのころにはまた、ピギービラーが我が子から離れようと急いで行くのにも出会う。子は砂に埋めて、自分でどうにかするように置いてきたのである。もう運んでやれない。子のとげが袋の中で刺し始めるからだ。それで置き去りにして急いで去り、その泣き声を聞かずに済むようにする。大きく育ったころにまた会えると分かっているのである。それからメイラーがやわらかく吹くにつれ、花が一つまた一つと開き、蜂がまた蜜を集めに出て来る。どの鳥もいちばん華やかな羽をまとい、いちばん甘い歌を歌って連れ合いを引き寄せ、番いになって巣を作りに行く。そしてメイラーはなおやわらかく吹き、大地が実りに満ちるまで続く。そのとき太陽のイーが、メイラーを来た方へ追い返し、花はうなだれ、鳥は明け方にしか歌わなくなる。嵐が過ぎて太陽を冷ますまで、イーがこの地を治めるからである。そして冬がその座に就き、みなに愛され実りをもたらすメイラーに、またも吹き払われるのである。
